title: Sen. Brian M. Chavez voted Yea on SB102, a tax foreclosure and land reutilization bill
text:
Sen. Brian M. Chavez voted Yea on SB102, a tax foreclosure and land reutilization bill
Sen. Brian M. Chavez (R-30th) voted Yea on SB102, a tax foreclosure and land reutilization bill, which passed the Ohio Senate 33-0 during the 136th Ohio General Assembly on Wednesday, June 10, 2026, according to the Ohio Legislature.
The following summary and breakdown are based on the bill's official text and may include interpretation to clarify the bill's provisions.
This bill overhauls Ohio’s tax foreclosure and land reutilization laws, renaming them the Gus Frangos Act. It refines county foreclosure procedures, expands the use of county boards of revision, and tightens notice, service and redemption rules, including an “alternative redemption period” and a new right for interested parties to demand public auction. It broadens protections and tools for county land reutilization corporations, clarifies lien priority and environmental liability limits, and adjusts distributions of sale proceeds. The bill also creates a temporary tax exemption and payment-in-lieu system for properties conveyed by land banks, and makes conforming changes across related tax, nuisance and environmental statutes.
SB102 was introduced by Sen. Thomas F. Patton.
Chavez is serving his first full term in the Ohio Senate, representing the 30th Senate District.
Prior to his appointment to the senate, Chavez was a member of the Oil and Gas Commission and held leadership roles in the Ohio Oil and Gas Association and Southeast Ohio Oil and Gas Association.
Chavez earned a degree in Chemical Engineering and worked at Intel Corporation before moving to Ohio.
He has been active in legislation during the 135th General Assembly, focusing on supporting military homeownership and infrastructure funding.
In Ohio, the legislative process begins when a bill is introduced in either the House of Representatives or the Senate. A bill must receive three considerations in each chamber, and it may be referred to a committee for hearings, debate and possible amendments before advancing to a floor vote. If both chambers pass the same version, the bill is sent to the governor, who can sign it, veto it or allow it to become law without a signature. The Ohio General Assembly begins a new legislative session every two years on the first Monday in January of odd-numbered years, and there is no limit on the number of days it may convene.
